title: Analysis of sparse cutting planes for sparse milps with applications to stochastic milps
contribution: Data-independent, mostly tight bounds on the ratio between the sparse-cut closure bound and the MILP optimum for packing, covering and general c>=0 MILPs, depending only on the sparsity pattern of the constraint matrix and the cut supports, with consequences for scenario-specific cuts in two-stage stochastic MILPs.
problem_entry: Solvers prefer sparse cuts and real MILPs are sparse (MIPLIB 2010 mean density 1.63%, median 0.17%), but cut selection has no theory; the paper is framed as a mathematical explanation of Crowder-Johnson-Padberg's sparse-cut observations (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Fix the cut supports, add all valid cuts on them (sparse closure), and bound z^cut/z^I by graph invariants of the constraint matrix: fractional mixed chromatic number of a packing interaction graph, mixed chromatic number of a covering interaction graph, corrected average density for general A (pp. 4-14).
assumptions: Packing/covering with nonnegative data, or arbitrary A with c>=0 and x>=0; mixed-integer variables; cuts are the strongest on each support (an idealisation of any cut family); block partition is a free choice; two-stage stochastic MILPs as running example (pp. 3-7, 11-14).
proof_devices: upper bound by patching conditional IP optima over mixed stable sets plus a fractional cover LP (Lemmas 33-34, Thm. 11; pp. 8-9, 18-20)
Brooks' theorem to pass to max degree (Cor. 12, p. 9; Thm. 35, p. 20)
BFS edge labelling of trees with 2Delta-1 labels covering each node Delta times (Lemma 36, Cor. 37; pp. 21-23)
tight instances from affine n-designs for prime n (Def. 38, Thm. 39; pp. 23-24, 27)
duplicated classical set-cover integrality-gap instance for the covering negative result (Def. 47, Lemma 49; p. 29)
product set system with non-empty intersections for the covering tightness construction (Lemmas 53-54; p. 32)
cycle bound split by length modulo 3 (Thm. 17, p. 11)
experiments: Small synthetic pure-binary instances (two-stage with 10 scenarios; random graphs nv=10), natural sparse closure computed exactly by IP-oracle row generation in CPLEX 12.5; observed ratios 1 to 1.009 against theoretical bounds 1.667 to 10 (pp. 15-17, 39-41).
positioning: Continues their own vertex-count geometric analysis with different techniques; explains Crowder-Johnson-Padberg 1983; gives what it calls the first global bounds on the nonanticipativity dual; links to two-stage matching approximation left to future work (pp. 1-3, 7, 11).
writing: Main results section before all proofs; each bound followed by a tightness theorem and a stochastic-programming corollary; a worked toy example before the proof; explicit hedges about sparsity of real instances (pp. 2-15).
limits_future: Super sparse cuts can be arbitrarily bad for covering (Thm. 18); bounds are worst case and experiments beat them; experiments small and synthetic; no bridge to an actual selection rule; two-stage matching link deferred (pp. 11-12, 15-18).

method_links.note: sparse-cut preference as unexplained habit, proxy = closure of all cuts on fixed supports, data-independent measure, return to data showing practice beats the bound
tightness theorem for nearly every bound and an explicit negative class (super sparse cuts for covering)
ground truth is the exactly computed sparse closure on small generated instances, compared with the theoretical bound rather than with a solver

Our main observation is the sparse cuts usually perform much better than the worst-case bounds we obtain theoretically.

title: Improving the randomization step in feasibility pump
contribution: A WalkSAT-inspired randomization step for Feasibility Pump based on minimal projected infeasibility certificates, with the first running-time bounds for an FP variant (decomposable mixed-binary sets; separable subset-sum for the full pump) and a conservative implementation that consistently improves Feasibility Pump 2.0.
problem_entry: FP succeeds in practice but its variants all keep the original randomization step and there are no running-time bounds; the paper targets that untouched component (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: When FP stalls, flip variables sampled from the support of a minimal projected certificate of infeasibility; minimality keeps the move inside one block of a decomposable instance (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: Mixed-binary sets; decomposable block structure as the analysis model; full FP analysed only on separable subset-sum with vertex projections and consistent rounding; the general case is called elusive (pp. 2-3, 7).
proof_devices: Schoening-style lucky-move argument on Hamming distance to a fixed feasible point, restarted in blocks of n iterations (Thm. 3.4, p. 6)
Fourier-Motzkin plus Caratheodory for certificates with at most d+1 rows, found by one LP (Lemma 3.2, p. 5; Appendix A, p. 16)
minimal certificate uses one block only, then union bound over blocks (Lemma 3.5, Thm. 3.3; pp. 6-7)
idempotence of project-plus-round on subset-sum by case analysis (Lemma 4.3, pp. 8-9)
coupling with a compressed algorithm at a factor-2 cost (Lemma 4.4, pp. 9-10)
two-flip lucky move requiring l=2 (Lemma 4.6, pp. 10-11)
counterexamples where original FP cycles (Remark 2.3, p. 3; Appendix B, pp. 16-17)
no long cycles under consistent rounding (Thm. 4.1, p. 7; Appendix C, pp. 17-18)
experiments: Analysed WFP lost to the original and was replaced by a conservative WFPbase; FP 2.0 with CPLEX 12.6.3, all other features unchanged, 10 seeds, half-hour limit; 50 random two-stage instances (+28% found, -17% time, -33% iterations) and 82 filtered MIPLIB 2010 models (+6%, -8.4%, -5.9%) with shifted geometric means (pp. 12-14).
positioning: Credits the FP literature and names its blind spot (randomization); claims the first running-time analysis of any FP variant; borrows WalkSAT/Schoening; reuses the decomposability lens of S024 (pp. 2-4).
writing: Separate contributions section with informal theorem statements and interpretation; proof sketch before each long proof; dead end reported with three reasons; strong closing recommendation (pp. 2-4, 12-13).
limits_future: Full FP analysis only for separable subset-sum; bounds exponential per block; implemented rule differs from the analysed one; no future-work section (pp. 3, 12).

method_links.note: FP randomization is a practice that works without theory; analysed on a proxy class (decomposable sets, subset-sum) and explained by sparsity and decomposability

against the 'step 8 rarely closed' limitation: a rule from the theory is implemented in a state-of-the-art code and recommended for all FP codes, after the analysed version failed and was made conservative
counterexamples where original randomization never converges; scope of the FP theorem stated as subset-sum only
instrument varies only the studied decision inside FP 2.0 with 10 seeds, but there is no exact ceiling to compare with

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge this is the first theoretical analysis of the running-time of a variant of Feasibility Pump algorithm, even for a special class of instances.
In preliminary tests, we implemented the algorithm WFP as described in the previous section. However, its performance was not competitive with FPorig.

title: Nonunique lifting of integer variables in minimal inequalities
contribution: A general theory for lifting integer variables in cut-generating functions without the unique lifting property: the fixing region after optimally lifting one column, a geometric inner approximation and universal upper bound, partial cut-generating pairs with an extension theorem, translation invariance of one-point fixability, and one-point fixability of mixing-set Type 3 triangles.
problem_entry: The S-free-set recipe gives only partially minimal pairs and the literature studies unique liftings; this paper takes the non-unique case, motivated by Section 7 of Dey-Wolsey 2010 (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Optimal lifting of one column equals the smallest apex height of a lattice-free pyramid over the S-free set; iterating the pyramid handles further columns, and blocking points with their spindles give a region where all optimal liftings agree (pp. 8-12).
assumptions: Closed S not containing 0 for the partial-pair theory; polyhedrally truncated affine lattices from Section 3; Type 3 triangles in R^2 with S = Z^2 + b for the application, with extra conditions on b for mixing-set triangles (pp. 4, 8, 14-17).
proof_devices: partial cut-generating pairs and an extension theorem under a cone condition, with a Gomory-Johnson negative case (Thm. 3, pp. 4-7)
infimum over conic combinations followed by Zorn's lemma to reach a minimal pair (pp. 6-7; Appendix A, p. 21)
lifted column turned into an extra continuous column of an (n+1)-dimensional model (Claim 8, Thm. 7; pp. 10-11)
unimodular map showing independence of integer height (Prop. 12, p. 13)
fundamental-region decomposition into five polytopes inside translated spindles (Claim 16, p. 16; Fig. 1, p. 17)
lattice-freeness by covering each slice with three split sets (Prop. 17, pp. 18-19)
pasting lemma, local finiteness, closedness and invariance of domain giving open+closed+nonempty = R^n (Appendix E, pp. 24-27)
positioning: Extends the unique-lifting literature to its complement; uses the Dey-Wolsey algebraic formula and the Basu et al. pyramid characterisation; re-derives a Dey-Wolsey result with more geometric techniques; notes later use of partial pairs by Basu et al. (pp. 2-4, 8, 17).
writing: Numbered statement-of-results list, guiding questions written as questions, technical proofs moved to appendices with stated reasons, open point named plainly, acknowledgement of a referee-found flaw (pp. 3-4, 12-14, 19).
limits_future: Equality of the inner approximation and the fixing region is open; one-point-fixability condition only sufficient and checked only for Type 3 triangles in R^2; no computation; no conclusion section (pp. 3, 15-18).

method_links.note: MILP side of the paradigm (S-free sets, cut-generating functions, lifting, two-row triangles) developed inside MILP rather than imported into QCQP; documents the toolbox of Method 3 step 1
negative case before the positive extension theorem; unresolved gap between inner approximation and fixing region stated; sufficient condition labelled as such
